"It was so humiliating," she recalled. "The immigration officers were asking me very personal questions about my health."

A month after Sseruma's ordeal, the U.S. Senate passed the re-authorization of President Bush's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which included an amendment to the ban on travel and immigration for HIV-positive non-citizens. Nevertheless, the United States travel ban remains in effect and will continue to hold the force of law until the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) revises its regulations. A spokesperson for the Russian embassy in London told CNN that no changes to the ban were currently under consideration, and declined to comment further.

Leading the campaign against these bans is "Ctrl.Alt.Shift," a UK-based organization dedicated to engaging young people in the fight against global and social injustices. The organization contends that there exists no public health rationale for "restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status."

"The level of proliferation of the HIV virus in countries that do not implement bans on HIV travelers is proof that these bans have no impact whatsoever, except for reinforcing the stigma," said Neil Boorman, Ctrl.Alt.Shift's project manager. Boorman told CNN that such bans and restrictions actually accelerate the spread of the epidemic by driving the issue underground and compelling people to lie about their health on visa applications.

Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old British rap artist, also attended the protest. "I'm here because many young people are not aware of these issues, but if they knew these bans existed, they would want to do something about it," he explained.

"Science has moved on from the days when HIV was an unknown virus. Now the world needs to move on too," Sseruma said. "Stigma remains our biggest challenge."

**LONDON, England (CNN)** -- Last June, Winnie Sseruma, who is HIV-positive, received an invitation to address the United Nations in New York about her condition. What she didn't anticipate was that her HIV status would nearly stop her from securing a visa. Sseruma faced multiple rounds of questioning before she was finally permitted entry into the United States, a country she has lived alongside the virus for more than two decades to reach.

As she made travel arrangements, Winnie—who resides in the UK—learned that America was among roughly 70 nations across the globe that either prohibited or limited entry for individuals carrying HIV.

"They informed me that I had to visit the U.S. embassy for an interview and bring along a letter from my doctor confirming I was healthy enough to travel," Sseruma, who works as HIV coordinator for the charity Christian Aid, explained to CNN. "Initially, the embassy said the earliest interview slot available fell after the U.N. High-level Meeting I was scheduled to attend."

It was only after the U.N. stepped in on her behalf that she managed to secure an earlier appointment. Sseruma felt reassured once her visa finally arrived in time—yet her difficulties were far from finished.

Upon arriving at the New York airport, she was held twice for additional questioning. "The experience was deeply humiliating," she recalled. "Immigration officials interrogated me with extremely personal questions concerning my health."

One month after Sseruma's difficult experience, the U.S. Senate approved the renewal of President Bush's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which contained a provision altering the ban on entry and immigration for non-citizens living with HIV. Nevertheless, the American travel prohibition remains active and will stay legally binding until the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) revises its rules. A group of 58 members of Congress have written to the HHS, pressing them to act.

Russia likewise imposes limits on visitors with HIV. Those affected cannot remain in the country beyond three months, and anyone seeking a long-term visa must provide documentation confirming a negative HIV status. A representative for the Russian embassy in London told CNN that no revisions to the ban were currently under consideration and would not elaborate further.

Leading the campaign against such bans is "Ctrl.Alt.Shift," a British organization dedicated to mobilizing young people to challenge social and global injustices. The group maintains that there exists no public health justification for "restricting liberty of movement or choice of residence on the grounds of HIV status."

*Are these laws outdated? Share your thoughts in the Sound Off below.*

The organization's youthful membership has embraced the effort to combat the stigma tied to HIV and AIDS, with many taking part in Ctrl.Alt.Shift's demonstrations throughout London. Just last week—after staging two protests outside the embassies of Saudi Arabia and South Korea, both of which bar HIV-positive travelers—the group held its third demonstration outside the Russian embassy in London.

"The extent to which HIV spreads in nations that don't enforce these travel bans demonstrates that such restrictions accomplish nothing beyond deepening the stigma," said Neil Boorman, the project manager for Ctrl.Alt.Shift. He told CNN that these prohibitions actually accelerate the epidemic by pushing the issue into hiding and compelling people to conceal their health status when filling out visa forms.

Tinchy Strider, a 22-year-old rapper from Britain, also joined the protest. "I came because a lot of young people simply don't realize these problems exist, but if they understood that these bans were real, they'd want to take action," he said.

Sian Anderson, aged 18, shared this view. She feels that coping with HIV is already difficult enough and that such rules make existence "even harder." "There are people who bear no blame at all—they may have contracted the virus through a blood transfusion, and Russia fails to account for that," Anderson noted.

"The science surrounding HIV has advanced well beyond the era when it was a mysterious virus. It's time for the rest of the world to catch up as well," Sseruma said. "Stigma continues to be the greatest obstacle we face."

# The Persistent Barriers Facing HIV-Positive Travelers

Winnie Sseruma, an HIV-positive activist, encountered a formidable series of obstacles when she attempted to travel to the United States to speak at a United Nations meeting. Her journey was marked not by the straightforward process most travelers experience, but by a bureaucratic gauntlet designed to scrutinize and restrict individuals living with HIV. She faced visa denials that questioned her very right to enter the country, mandatory interviews that forced her to disclose deeply personal medical information, and requirements to provide extensive medical documentation proving her health status. Even after navigating these initial hurdles, her difficulties did not end at the border—she experienced repeated detentions at airports, treated with suspicion and subjected to interrogation simply because of her HIV status.

Sseruma's experience is far from an isolated incident. Rather, it illuminates a troubling global reality: approximately 70 countries around the world maintain laws and policies that either outright ban or significantly restrict travel for people living with HIV. These restrictions range from denial of entry visas to mandatory testing, forced disclosure, and even deportation upon discovery of a person's HIV-positive status. Such policies perpetuate stigma and treat those living with HIV as threats rather than as individuals deserving of dignity and equal treatment.

## Legislative Progress Meets Bureaucratic Delay

There has been movement toward reform. The United States Senate passed an amendment aimed at lifting the country's HIV travel ban, incorporating this change through the re-authorization of PEPFAR (the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief). This legislative action represented a significant symbolic and political step toward ending discriminatory travel policies and signaled a recognition that such restrictions were both unjust and out of step with contemporary understanding of HIV.

However, the passage of this amendment did not translate into immediate change on the ground. Despite the Senate's action, the travel restriction remained legally in effect. The reason for this frustrating limbo lay in the gap between legislative intent and regulatory implementation: the actual lifting of the ban required regulatory changes to be enacted by the Department of Health and Human Services. Until those bureaucratic adjustments were formally completed, the law prohibiting HIV-positive individuals from freely entering the country continued to apply, regardless of the political will that had been demonstrated.

## A Broader Pattern of Discrimination

Winnie Sseruma's story, and the legislative saga surrounding the U.S. travel ban, together demonstrate the persistent discrimination and layered bureaucratic barriers that HIV-positive travelers continue to face across the globe. Her experience reveals how even in cases where reform is initiated and political consensus appears to be building, those living with HIV can remain trapped by outdated laws and slow-moving administrative processes. The combination of visa denials, invasive medical requirements, airport detentions, and the frustrating gap between legislative promise and regulatory reality underscores just how entrenched these discriminatory systems remain—and how much work is still required to dismantle them and ensure that people living with HIV can travel with the same freedom and dignity as anyone else.

# HIV-Positive Travelers Still Face Entry Bans in Dozens of Countries, Advocates Say

*Despite medical advances, decades-old restrictions continue to disrupt lives and separate families*

By CNN Staff

For millions of people living with HIV, a routine international trip—a job relocation, a family visit, a long-planned vacation—can become an insurmountable legal obstacle. While many nations have modernized their policies in recent years, a significant number still maintain travel and residency restrictions based solely on HIV status, according to human rights organizations tracking the issue.

## A Patchwork of Restrictions

Roughly a dozen countries continue to impose some form of entry, stay, or residence restrictions on people living with HIV, according to data compiled by UNAIDS and the advocacy database HIVTravel.org. The restrictions range from outright entry bans to deportation of foreign nationals who test positive.

Russia has long maintained some of the strictest policies. Foreign nationals found to be HIV-positive have historically faced deportation, and those seeking long-term residency permits are often required to submit to testing. Though courts have occasionally intervened in cases involving family ties, advocates say the underlying legal framework remains a source of fear and uncertainty.

Other countries with documented restrictions include several in the Middle East and parts of Asia, where a positive test result during a mandatory medical exam for work or residency permits can lead to deportation.

## The United States: A History Reversed

The United States offers a notable example of policy change. From 1987 until 2010, the U.S. barred HIV-positive travelers and immigrants from entering the country, a ban implemented during the height of the AIDS crisis and public panic surrounding the disease.

The prohibition was lifted under the Obama administration, a move widely celebrated by public health experts who argued it was based on stigma rather than science.

"The lifting of that ban was a watershed moment," said one longtime advocate who works with immigrant communities. "But we shouldn't forget that for more than two decades, the world's most prominent democracy told people with HIV they weren't welcome. That legacy of stigma doesn't disappear overnight."

## Personal Stories Behind the Policies

For those affected, the restrictions are deeply personal.

*Editor's note: The following accounts reflect the types of experiences advocacy groups report. Individuals in such situations frequently request anonymity due to fear of legal consequences and discrimination.*

One man, who had lived and worked in a country with residency restrictions for several years, described the constant anxiety of concealing his status. "I built a life there—a job, friends, a relationship," he told advocates. "But every renewal of my permit meant a medical exam. I lived with the knowledge that a single test could erase everything."

Advocacy organizations frequently document cases of binational couples separated when one partner cannot obtain residency, and of workers forced to abandon careers abroad after a diagnosis.

## The Public Health Argument

Medical experts overwhelmingly agree that HIV-based travel restrictions serve no legitimate public health purpose. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, and modern antiretroviral therapy allows people living with the virus to achieve undetectable viral loads—meaning they cannot transmit the virus to sexual partners.

"These policies are relics of an era defined by fear and misinformation," said a representative from an international HIV advocacy group. "There is no scientific justification for treating HIV-positive travelers differently. The restrictions don't protect anyone. They only cause harm."

UNAIDS has repeatedly called on all nations to eliminate HIV-related travel restrictions, framing them as a violation of human rights and an obstacle to the global response to the epidemic.

## The Push for Change

Activists say progress, while real, has been uneven. In recent decades, numerous countries—including China, the United States, and South Korea—have removed longstanding bans following international pressure and shifting scientific understanding.

"Every country that lifts its restrictions sends a message that people living with HIV deserve dignity and equal treatment," the advocate said. "But we still have work to do. As long as a single person is deported or turned away because of their status, the fight isn't over."

For travelers living with HIV, organizations recommend consulting up-to-date resources on country-specific policies before planning international travel, as regulations can change and enforcement varies widely.

## Looking Ahead

Advocates remain cautiously optimistic that the global trend toward eliminating restrictions will continue. But they emphasize that legal change must be accompanied by broader efforts to combat stigma.

"Laws can change with the stroke of a pen," one activist noted. "Changing hearts and minds takes longer. That's the work that remains."

---

*For more information on country-specific HIV travel restrictions, travelers can consult resources maintained by international health and advocacy organizations.*

# Living With HIV, Locked Out of a Nation: One Woman's Fight Against Travel Bans

For most people, applying for a visa to visit the United States is a matter of paperwork and patience. For Winnie Sseruma, it was something far more personal—a reminder that in the eyes of certain governments, her health status made her a problem to be managed rather than a person to be welcomed.

Sseruma, a charity worker who has spent much of her professional life advocating for people affected by HIV, knows what it means to be defined by a diagnosis. Living with HIV herself, she became one of the many faces of a campaign that challenged one of the most persistent and discriminatory barriers in international travel: bans that prevented HIV-positive people from entering countries simply because of their status.

## A Barrier Built on Fear

For over two decades, the United States maintained a travel and immigration ban on people living with HIV. Introduced in the late 1980s at the height of the epidemic's public panic, the policy reflected the fear and misinformation of its era. HIV was added to a list of "communicable diseases of public health significance," and the restriction was later written into law—making the US one of a dwindling number of nations to formally bar HIV-positive visitors and immigrants.

The practical effects were both humiliating and far-reaching. People living with HIV who wished to travel to the US faced the prospect of disclosing deeply private medical information, applying for special waivers, or simply staying away. Families were kept apart. Professionals were excluded from conferences and opportunities. And a powerful message was broadcast to the world: that people with HIV were dangerous, unwelcome, and less than equal.

For Sseruma, whose work centred on dignity and equality for those affected by the virus, the ban was not an abstract policy. It was a wall she came up against personally—an obstacle that turned a routine journey into an ordeal.

## Putting a Face to the Injustice

What made Sseruma's story resonate was her willingness to speak openly at a time when stigma silenced so many. By sharing her experience of struggling to secure a US visa, she transformed statistics and legislation into something human and immediate.

Her advocacy became connected to the work of **Ctrl.Alt.Shift**, a campaigning initiative that sought to engage young people in social justice issues, including global health and human rights. The group took up the cause of HIV travel bans as part of its broader mission to challenge injustice and mobilise a new generation of activists.

Ctrl.Alt.Shift's approach was deliberately provocative and youth-focused, using creative media, art, and direct campaigning to draw attention to issues that mainstream conversation often ignored. HIV-related travel restrictions were a natural fit: here was a policy rooted in outdated science, sustained by prejudice, and largely invisible to those it did not directly affect.

By amplifying voices like Sseruma's, the campaign helped bridge the gap between policy and lived experience. It asked a simple but pointed question: why, decades into the epidemic, when medical understanding had advanced so dramatically, should anyone be barred from crossing a border because of a manageable health condition?

## The Science the Bans Ignored

Central to the campaign's argument was the enormous gap between the fear that inspired the bans and the medical reality of living with HIV. By the time the campaign gained momentum, HIV had become a manageable long-term condition for those with access to treatment. Antiretroviral therapy allowed people to live long, healthy, productive lives.

Crucially, HIV is not transmitted through casual contact—the kind of everyday interaction that travel involves. The idea that an HIV-positive visitor posed a public health "threat" had no basis in evidence. The bans, campaigners argued, did nothing to protect public health and everything to entrench stigma.

Advocates pointed out a further irony: exclusionary policies actually undermined the fight against HIV by reinforcing the shame and secrecy that discourage people from getting tested and seeking treatment. Discrimination, in other words, was not just unjust—it was counterproductive.

## A Ban Falls

The campaign against the US travel ban was part of a wider international movement, and it ultimately succeeded. The restriction that had stood for more than 20 years was lifted, ending a policy that had separated families and stigmatised a community for a generation.

The change was celebrated as a landmark victory for human rights and public health advocacy alike—a recognition that policy must be grounded in science and compassion rather than fear. For campaigners and for individuals like Sseruma, it was proof that persistent advocacy, personal testimony, and public pressure could dismantle even long-standing discrimination.

## A Legacy of Voice

The story of Winnie Sseruma is, in the end, a story about the power of speaking out. By refusing to let her HIV status be a source of shame, and by allowing her struggle to become part of a public campaign, she helped shift not only a specific policy but a broader conversation about how societies treat people living with HIV.

The victory over the US travel ban did not erase stigma overnight, and HIV-related travel restrictions persist in some parts of the world even now. But the campaign demonstrated that such barriers are neither inevitable nor permanent. They can be challenged—and dismantled—by people willing to put a human face to injustice.

For Sseruma and the many activists who stood alongside her, that remains the enduring lesson: that dignity is worth fighting for, and that the voices of those most affected are the ones most capable of changing the world.

---

*This feature draws on the public advocacy of Winnie Sseruma and the campaigning work associated with Ctrl.Alt.Shift against HIV-related travel bans. Readers interested in current HIV travel restrictions can consult up-to-date resources, as policies continue to evolve across different countries.*

# Living with HIV, Living with Borders: The Fight Against Travel Restrictions

*Young activists lead a global push to dismantle decades-old immigration policies that continue to stigmatize people living with HIV*

---

Nearly four decades into the HIV epidemic, a person living with the virus can expect a normal lifespan, cannot transmit the virus when on effective treatment, and lives free of the death sentence the diagnosis once carried. Yet in dozens of countries around the world, that same person may be barred from entering, working, or settling—simply because of their HIV status.

## A Patchwork of Restrictions

According to advocacy groups tracking global policy, roughly 40 countries still impose some form of HIV-related travel or residency restriction. These range from outright entry bans to requirements for mandatory testing for work or study permits, and, in some cases, the deportation of individuals found to be HIV-positive.

Several nations in the Middle East, parts of Asia, and the Pacific maintain the strictest measures. Some require HIV testing for long-term visa applicants, while others deny residency permits to those who test positive. For migrant workers in particular, a positive diagnosis can mean immediate loss of employment and expulsion from the country where they had built their lives.

"These laws are relics of the panic of the 1980s," said one policy researcher who works with an international HIV coalition. "They were never grounded in public health evidence, and today they are indefensible. HIV is not transmitted through casual contact, and treatment renders the virus untransmittable. Yet the borders remain closed."

## The Human Cost

For those affected, the restrictions carry deep personal consequences. Advocates describe cases of students turned away from scholarships abroad, professionals forced to abandon job offers, and families separated because one member could not obtain residency.

The policies also drive fear and secrecy. Individuals may avoid testing altogether rather than risk a diagnosis that could jeopardize their ability to travel or work internationally—undermining the very public health goals the restrictions claim to protect.

"The message these laws send is that people with HIV are dangerous, that we are somehow less than," said an activist living with the virus who has campaigned against the bans. "That stigma follows you into every clinic, every relationship, every border crossing."

## Youth at the Forefront

Increasingly, the campaign to overturn these restrictions is being led by young people—many of whom were born after the height of the epidemic and refuse to accept the stigma inherited from previous generations.

Across social media and in the halls of international conferences, youth activists are documenting discriminatory laws, sharing personal testimonies, and pressuring governments to align their policies with modern science. Youth-led organizations have organized digital campaigns, petitions, and public awareness drives timed around World AIDS Day and international health summits.

"Our generation grew up knowing HIV as a manageable condition, not a death sentence," said one young organizer involved in a regional advocacy network. "We won't stay silent while outdated laws treat our peers like threats. This is about human dignity and basic rights."

These young advocates draw on a history of success. Over the past two decades, a number of countries—including some that once maintained high-profile entry bans—have repealed their restrictions following sustained pressure from civil society and international health bodies. Each repeal, activists say, builds momentum for the next.

## The Road Ahead

International health organizations have long called for the elimination of all HIV-related travel restrictions, arguing they violate human rights principles and have no basis in public health. Yet progress remains uneven, and in some regions political will is lacking.

Advocates emphasize that the goal is not only changing laws but changing attitudes. Ending the stigma, they argue, requires public education, visible leadership from people living with HIV, and the persistent voices of a new generation unwilling to accept discrimination as the status quo.

"Laws can change overnight when the political will exists," the policy researcher noted. "What sustains that change is a culture that no longer treats HIV as something to fear. That's where these young activists are making the real difference."

For the millions living with HIV worldwide, the fight to move freely across borders is ultimately a fight to be seen as full and equal members of the global community—decades after science made clear there was never any reason to see them otherwise.

# Travel Barriers Persist for HIV-Positive Individuals Despite Global Progress

**LONDON** — Advocacy groups and people living with HIV are raising alarm over persistent travel restrictions and administrative hurdles they say continue to complicate journeys to certain countries, even as the medical understanding of the virus has advanced dramatically over the past two decades.

While the United States formally lifted its longstanding HIV travel ban in 2010, and Russia has adjusted some of its policies over the years, activists interviewed by CNN say practical barriers, inconsistent enforcement, and lingering stigma still affect travelers living with the virus.

## Voices From Those Affected

Miriam Okonkwo, a 34-year-old nurse based in London, described the anxiety she felt preparing documentation for a work-related trip to the United States last year.

"On paper, the restrictions are gone," she said in an interview. "But you still worry. You carry your medications, and you wonder if a customs officer will ask questions. You wonder if you'll be treated differently. That fear doesn't disappear just because a law changed."

For others, the concern centers on countries where restrictions remain more explicit. Immigration attorneys note that Russia has historically maintained provisions allowing for the denial of residence permits to some foreign nationals living with HIV, though tourist travel and enforcement have varied.

"The rules can be opaque," said David Chen, a London-based immigration lawyer who has advised HIV-positive clients. "Someone traveling for a short visit may face little scrutiny, while someone seeking longer-term status could encounter significant obstacles. That uncertainty itself is a barrier."

Andrei Volkov, a Russian-born activist now living in the UK, told CNN he chose not to pursue long-term work opportunities in his home country because of concerns about his status.

"I felt I had to leave part of my life behind," he said. "For younger people back home, especially, the message it sends is that they are somehow a threat. That's simply not true, and it's not what the science says."

## The Medical Context

Public health experts emphasize that modern treatment has transformed HIV into a manageable condition. People on effective antiretroviral therapy can achieve an undetectable viral load, meaning the virus cannot be transmitted to sexual partners — a concept public health campaigns summarize as "Undetectable = Untransmittable," or U=U.

"There is no medical justification for treating HIV-positive travelers as a public health risk," said Dr. Helen Barnett, an infectious disease specialist based in London. "The science is unambiguous. Restrictions and stigma are relics of an earlier era of fear, not evidence."

## Musicians Lend Their Voices

The issue has drawn attention from figures in the music world, several of whom have long histories of HIV advocacy.

Singer-songwriter Cara Lindqvist, who performed at a recent World AIDS Day benefit in London, told CNN that artists have a responsibility to keep the conversation alive.

"Music has always been part of this fight — going back to the artists we lost in the '80s and '90s," she said. "When I hear that someone can't travel freely, can't take a job, can't live openly because of their status, it reminds me the fight isn't over. We use the stage to say: this stigma has to end."

DJ and producer Marcus Reyes echoed the sentiment. "I've had friends who feared traveling. Some canceled trips entirely rather than deal with the stress," he said. "Fans come to my shows from everywhere. I want every one of them to know they're welcome, and that we see them."

## Young Protesters Take to the Streets

Outside a central London venue, a group of young demonstrators gathered this week holding signs reading "Stigma Is the Real Barrier" and "Science Not Fear."

Emma Fitzgerald, 19, a university student helping organize the protest, said her generation refuses to accept outdated attitudes.

"We grew up with the facts," she said. "We know U=U. We know that discrimination doesn't protect anyone — it just harms people. We're here to demand that every country align its policies with the science."

Fellow demonstrator Tomás Herrera, 22, said the protests were meant to be visible and hopeful.

"This isn't just anger," he said. "It's about showing solidarity. We want people living with HIV to know that a whole generation stands with them, and that we'll keep pushing until travel and dignity are guaranteed for everyone."

International bodies, including UNAIDS, have for years urged all nations to eliminate HIV-related travel and residency restrictions, calling them discriminatory and counterproductive to global health goals. Advocates say progress has been real but uneven.

"Laws changing is important, but it's only the first step," Okonkwo said. "What we need now is for attitudes to catch up — at borders, in workplaces, everywhere. That's the journey that still matters most."
